# 1. Import Dataset

```{r}
# Import the stock market dataset
my_stocks <- read.csv(
  "stocks.csv",
  header = TRUE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Display first few rows
head(my_stocks)
```

# 2. Data Preparation

```{r}

# Load required libraries
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Check structure of the dataset
str(my_stocks)

# Display summary of the dataset
summary(my_stocks)

# Display column names
colnames(my_stocks)

# Display first 10 rows
head(my_stocks, 10)
```

The CSV file has been loaded using the `read.csv()` function. The dataset contains stock market information such as stock symbol, date, opening price, highest price, lowest price, closing price, trading volume and adjusted closing price.

The `str()` function is used to understand the structure of the dataset, while `summary()` provides a statistical summary of the columns. The `head()` function displays the first few records.

# 3. Convert Date and Numeric Columns

```{r}

# Convert date column into Date format
my_stocks$date <- as.Date(my_stocks$date)

# List of numeric columns
numeric_cols <- c(
  "stock_price_open",
  "stock_price_high",
  "stock_price_low",
  "stock_price_close",
  "stock_volume",
  "stock_price_adj_close"
)

# Convert numeric columns to numeric format
for(col in numeric_cols) {
  my_stocks[[col]] <- as.numeric(my_stocks[[col]])
}

# Check structure after conversion
str(my_stocks)
```

The date column is converted into proper Date format so that it can be used for time-based analysis and graphs.

The stock price and volume columns are also converted into numeric format.

# 4. Check Missing Values

```{r}

# Count missing values in each column
colSums(is.na(my_stocks))
```

The `is.na()` function is used to identify missing values in the dataset.

# 5. Remove Missing Values

```{r}

my_stocks <- my_stocks %>%
  drop_na(
    stock_symbol,
    date,
    stock_price_open,
    stock_price_high,
    stock_price_low,
    stock_price_close,
    stock_volume
  )

# Check the cleaned dataset
head(my_stocks)
```

Rows containing missing values in important stock-related columns are removed so that they do not affect the analysis.

# 6. Number of Different Stocks

```{r}

num_stocks <- my_stocks %>%
  summarise(
    n_stocks = n_distinct(stock_symbol)
  )

num_stocks
```

The `n_distinct()` function is used to calculate the number of unique stock symbols present in the dataset.

# 7. List of Different Stocks

```{r}

unique_stocks <- my_stocks %>%
  distinct(stock_symbol) %>%
  arrange(stock_symbol)

unique_stocks
```

The `distinct()` function is used to identify the unique stock symbols. The `arrange()` function sorts the stock symbols alphabetically.

# 8. Calculate Daily Price Change

```{r}

my_stocks <- my_stocks %>%
  arrange(stock_symbol, date) %>%
  group_by(stock_symbol) %>%
  mutate(
    daily_change = stock_price_close -
                   lag(stock_price_close)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

head(my_stocks)
```

The daily change is calculated by subtracting the previous day's closing price from the current day's closing price.

The `lag()` function is used to obtain the previous day's closing price.

# 9. Highest Single-Day Gain

```{r}

highest_gain <- my_stocks %>%
  filter(!is.na(daily_change)) %>%
  filter(daily_change == max(daily_change)) %>%
  select(
    stock_symbol,
    date,
    daily_change
  )

highest_gain
```

This identifies the stock that experienced the highest single-day increase in closing price and the date on which it occurred.

# 10. Highest Single-Day Loss

```{r}

highest_loss <- my_stocks %>%
  filter(!is.na(daily_change)) %>%
  filter(daily_change == min(daily_change)) %>%
  select(
    stock_symbol,
    date,
    daily_change
  )

highest_loss
```

This identifies the stock that experienced the highest single-day decrease in closing price and the date on which it occurred.

# 11. Visualization 1 - XOM Closing Price Over Time

```{r}

xom_data <- my_stocks %>%
  filter(stock_symbol == "XOM")

ggplot(
  xom_data,
  aes(
    x = date,
    y = stock_price_close
  )
) +
  geom_line(
    color = "blue",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "XOM Closing Price Over Time",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Closing Price"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

This graph shows the movement of XOM's closing price over time.

# 13. Visualization 3 - XOM Open vs Closing Price

```{r}

ggplot(
  xom_data,
  aes(x = date)
) +
  geom_line(
    aes(
      y = stock_price_open,
      color = "Opening Price"
    ),
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(
      y = stock_price_close,
      color = "Closing Price"
    ),
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "XOM Opening Price vs Closing Price",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Price",
    color = "Price Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

This graph compares XOM's opening price and closing price for each trading day.

# 15. Visualization 5 - XOM Trading Volume

```{r}

    y = stock_volume
  )
) +
  geom_line(
    color = "darkgreen",

```

This graph shows the number of shares traded for XOM over time.

# 16. Average Closing Price of Stocks

```{r}

average_close <- my_stocks %>%
  group_by(stock_symbol) %>%
  summarise(
    average_closing_price =
      mean(stock_price_close, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(average_closing_price))

head(average_close, 10)
```

This calculates the average closing price for each stock in the dataset.

# 17. Visualization 6 - Top 10 Stocks by Average Closing Price

```{r}

top_10_stocks <- average_close %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)

ggplot(
  top_10_stocks,
  aes(
    x = reorder(
      stock_symbol,
      average_closing_price
    ),
    y = average_closing_price
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 Stocks by Average Closing Price",
    x = "Stock Symbol",
    y = "Average Closing Price"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

This bar chart compares the average closing prices of the top 10 stocks.

# 18. Final Results

```{r}

cat("=====================================\n")
cat("       STOCK MARKET ANALYSIS\n")
cat("=====================================\n\n")

cat(
  "Number of different stocks:",
  num_stocks$n_stocks,
  "\n\n"
)

cat("Highest Single-Day Gain:\n")
print(highest_gain)

cat("\nHighest Single-Day Loss:\n")
print(highest_loss)
```

# 19. Conclusion

The stock market dataset was successfully imported and analyzed using R.

The analysis included data preparation, identification of different stocks, calculation of daily price changes, identification of the highest single-day gain and loss, and visualization of stock price and trading volume.

The visualizations provide a clear understanding of stock price movements, opening and closing prices, high and low prices, trading volume, and average closing prices.
